Let

\[
m=n^3.
\]

For each subset \(A\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,n\}\), write

\[
S_A=\sum_{i\in A}x_i.
\]

We first translate the condition in the problem into a condition on subset sums.

Suppose two different subsets \(A\neq B\) have the same sum modulo \(m\):

\[
S_A\equiv S_B \pmod{m}.
\]

Define \(\varepsilon_i\) by

\[
\varepsilon_i=
\begin{cases}
1,&i\in A\setminus B,\\
-1,&i\in B\setminus A,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(A\neq B\), not all \(\varepsilon_i\) are zero. But

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i x_i
= S_A-S_B\equiv 0 \pmod{m},
\]

which is forbidden. Therefore all \(2^n\) subset sums \(S_A\) must be pairwise distinct modulo \(n^3\).

There are only \(n^3\) residue classes modulo \(n^3\), so we must have

\[
2^n\le n^3.
\]

Now check when this inequality can hold. We have

\[
2^{10}=1024>1000=10^3.
\]

Also, for \(n\ge 10\),

\[
\frac{2^{n+1}}{(n+1)^3}
>
\frac{2n^3}{(n+1)^3}
=
\frac{2}{(1+1/n)^3}.
\]

Since \((1+1/n)^3\le (11/10)^3<2\), we get \(2^{n+1}>(n+1)^3\). Thus if the inequality fails at \(n=10\), it fails for all larger \(n\). Hence any admissible \(n\) must satisfy

\[
n\le 9.
\]

It remains to show that \(n=9\) is actually possible.

Take

\[
x_i=2^{i-1}\qquad (i=1,2,\dots,9).
\]

These are positive integers, so certainly nonnegative and not all zero. Their total sum is

\[
1+2+4+\cdots+256=511<729=9^3.
\]

For any choice of \(\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,0,1\}\), define

\[
A=\{i:\varepsilon_i=1\},\qquad B=\{i:\varepsilon_i=-1\}.
\]

Then

\[
\sum_{i=1}^9 \varepsilon_i x_i
=
\sum_{i\in A}2^{i-1}-\sum_{i\in B}2^{i-1}.
\]

All subset sums of powers of \(2\) are distinct, so if \(\varepsilon\) is not the zero vector, then \(A\neq B\), and the above integer is nonzero. Its absolute value is at most

\[
1+2+\cdots+256=511<729.
\]

Therefore it cannot be divisible by \(729=9^3\).

Thus \(n=9\) works, while no \(n\ge 10\) can work.

\[
\boxed{9}
\]

27B·v4.method: Equivalence to distinct subset sums yields 2^n ≤ n^3 upper bound; construction via powers of 2 achieves n=9.
